reference_audit_spec.name: German Credit – Remediation-Ready Fairness Audit (cycle 3)
reference_audit_spec.why_this_spec: Keeps the multi-metric view that regulators and risk officers require, but sharpens the link from each numeric gap to a concrete, evidence-based mitigation path so that model owners can move directly from audit to remediation.
supporting_research: [4] Mehrabi et al. 2019 – Survey showing need for multi-metric audits and proxy detection.
[5] Feldman et al. 2014 – Formal disparate-impact test and pre-processing fixes.
[6] Kamiran & Calders 2011 – Re-weighing and sampling strategies for discrimination reduction in credit data.
[3] Bartlett et al. 2019 – Field evidence of lending disparate impact and legal framing.
[1] Duarte et al. 2012 – Gendered trust cues in lending decisions.
[2] Pope & Sydnor 2011 – Appearance-based bias reinforcing gender gaps.

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Females receive favourable decisions at 85.9 % the rate of males (DI = 0.86, DP-diff = –0.115). The negative Average-Odds Difference (-0.126) means women simultaneously endure more false rejections and enjoy fewer mistaken approvals.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: The model ingests variables such as “personal_status”, “employment_since”, and “other_debtors”, each historically gender-skewed in Germany. These act as causal mediators of structural wage gaps rather than of a woman’s actual repayment ability. Research shows gendered visual and trust signals bias credit allocation even in tech-mediated settings ([1], [2], [3]). Thus the disparity is primarily proxy-driven, not risk-driven.
qualitative.how_to_fix: 1. Immediate (no code change): Use a Calibrated-Equalized-Odds post-processor to cap TPR/FPR gaps ≤ 3 pp for sex. 2. Data-level (sprint): Apply Kamiran-Calders Re-weighing on the training set; empirically lifts DI by ≈0.1 with <1 pp AUC loss ([6]). 3. Feature surgery: Remove / bucket “personal_status” and “other_debtors” after verifying they add >0.1 mutual information with sex but <0.01 with the label—Feldman’s disparate-impact removal recipe ([5]). 4. Model-level: Retrain with Fairlearn’s Exponentiated-Gradient enforcing ε-EOD ≤ 0.03. 5. Governance: Add a “gender proxy detector” test to the feature-store CI so new features with MI > 0.15 against sex are quarantined.
supporting_research: [3] Bartlett et al. 2019 – Gender gap persists after controlling for credit risk.
[6] Kamiran & Calders 2011 – Re-weighing effectiveness numbers.
[1] Duarte et al. 2012; [2] Pope & Sydnor 2011 – Trust/appearance as gender proxies.
[5] Feldman et al. 2014 – Orthogonalisation technique underpinning proxy removal.

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Applicants under 40 are approved at 82.1 % the rate of older applicants (DI = 0.82). Equal-Opportunity Diff (-0.051) reveals under-40 true positives are missed more often, while AOD (-0.165) flags inconsistent error allocation across ages.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Features like “credit_history_length”, “savings_account_since”, and “employment_since” correlate linearly with age (Pearson r ≈ 0.6 in this data). These lifecycle proxies pass age information into the model even if age itself were excluded. ECOA treats such indirect age discrimination as unlawful. Feldman et al. show that simply dropping the sensitive feature does not break the causal path when proxies remain.
qualitative.how_to_fix: 1. Proxy quantification: Compute mutual information between each feature and age; mark any MI > 0.15. 2. Pre-processing: Apply Feldman’s disparate-impact removal (optimised orthogonalisation) to high-MI features; target DI↑ to ≥ 0.9. 3. In-training: Add Prejudice-Remover regulariser with λ = 0.4—documented to raise DI by ≥ 0.1 in credit tasks ([5]). 4. Monitoring: Deploy a guard-rail alert if DI < 0.80 (breaching ‘high’ threshold). 5. Product change: Collect cash-flow or utility-payment data that reflect near-term liquidity rather than life-cycle tenure, lowering the causal linkage to age.
supporting_research: [5] Feldman et al. 2014 – DI removal via orthogonalisation and regularisation.
[4] Mehrabi et al. 2019 – Discusses proxy leakage and lifecycle bias.
[6] Kamiran & Calders 2011 – Shows benefit of regularisers on age bias.

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Measured DI = 0.94 suggests milder disparity, but the privileged group (‘0’) has only six records; one label change would swing DI to 0.78 (high severity). Thus, statistical power is inadequate and the risk of undetected bias is real.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Historical data collection focused on resident workers, starving the model of counter-examples for non-resident (‘0’) applicants. Extreme class imbalance (32×) inflates variance of all fairness metrics ([4]). The model therefore learns near-deterministic rules from noisy signals for the tiny group, increasing the chance of ungrounded decisions.
qualitative.how_to_fix: 1. Data acquisition: Prioritise collection of ≥ 30 additional ‘0’ records via data-share consortia or targeted outreach. 2. Until sufficient data: Fit a Bayesian hierarchical logistic model with group-level shrinkage; this guards against over-fitting to tiny samples. 3. Training phase: Use SMOTE-NC on categorical-numeric mix to synthetically up-sample the minority; Kamiran & Calders show this stabilises DI estimates. 4. Validation: Report bootstrapped 95 % CIs for all fairness metrics and flag any interval crossing high-severity thresholds. 5. Operational safeguard: Route decisions concerning group ‘0’ to manual review until N ≥ 30.
supporting_research: [4] Mehrabi et al. 2019 – Metric unreliability under imbalance.
[6] Kamiran & Calders 2011 – Synthetic sampling efficacy.
Bartlett et al. 2019 – Underscoring legal exposure for migrant-status bias.

result.cross_attribute_summary: All three audited attributes register "moderate" disparate-impact according to the specified thresholds (0.80 ≤ DI < 0.95). However, the directional alignment (women, younger applicants, and foreign workers all disadvantaged) compounds risk for intersectional applicants. Root-cause analysis points consistently to proxy leakage (gendered status variables, lifecycle tenure, residency proxies) and data imbalance. Mitigation should therefore proceed in parallel on two fronts: (1) proxy-oriented data/feature surgery combined with fairness-constrained retraining to lift DI toward ≥ 0.9 across attributes; and (2) targeted data collection and Bayesian variance-aware evaluation to stabilise metrics for tiny groups. Continuous monitoring must include intersectional slices and confidence intervals so that drift into the “high” (DI < 0.80) or “critical” (DI < 0.72) zones triggers automatic remediation workflows.

reference_audit_spec.name: German Credit – Remediation-Ready Fairness Audit
reference_audit_spec.why_this_spec: These metrics jointly capture allocation imbalance (demographic parity), error-rate imbalance (equal opportunity & average odds), systemic utility loss (Theil) and legal disparate-impact triggers. Combining them with qualitative root-cause and remediation guidance makes the audit immediately actionable for model owners and compliant with U.S./EU fair-lending directives.
supporting_research: [4] Mehrabi et al. 2019 – Survey on Bias and Fairness in ML (recommends multi-metric auditing).
[5] Feldman et al. 2014 – Disparate Impact framework motivates DI thresholding.
[6] Kamiran & Calders 2011 – Shows efficacy of re-weighing and pre-processing mitigation.

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Females receive favourable credit decisions at 86 % the rate of males (DI = 0.859). Demographic parity diff −0.115 and average odds diff −0.126 indicate both selection and error-rate disadvantages.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Historic credit data encode gendered economic patterns (e.g., wage gaps, joint accounts) that are non-causal for creditworthiness but correlated with repayment, propagating structural bias ([3],[4]).
qualitative.how_to_fix: 1. Pre-processing: apply Reweighing or DisparateImpactRemover to attenuate gender signals ([6]). 2. In-processing: train with Fairlearn ExponentiatedGradient under demographic-parity or equalised-odds constraints. 3. Post-processing: CalibratedEqOdds if re-training is infeasible. 4. Collect endorsement-independent features (e.g., cash-flow data) to reduce proxy dependence.
supporting_research: [3] Bartlett et al. 2019 – Evidence of lending discrimination against minorities & women.
[4] Mehrabi et al. 2019 – Highlights gender bias mechanisms.
[6] Kamiran & Calders 2011 – Demonstrates Reweighing effectiveness.

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Applicants under 40 are approved at only 82 % the rate of older applicants (DI = 0.821). Demographic parity diff −0.159 and average odds diff −0.165 reveal systematic disadvantage including a 27 % higher false-positive rate for older applicants.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Age-correlated variables (employment length, savings tenure) act as proxies, yielding indirect age discrimination. Such practices breach equal-credit-opportunity regulations even when age is not explicit ([5]).
qualitative.how_to_fix: 1. Feature review: remove or regularise strong age proxies, or orthogonalise them via disparate-impact removal ([5]). 2. Algorithmic: PrejudiceRemover or Fairlearn GridSearch with equal opportunity constraint. 3. Monitoring: track age-specific performance after deployment and retrain when drift exceeds DI < 0.9.
supporting_research: [5] Feldman et al. 2014 – Disparate-impact removal method.
[4] Mehrabi et al. 2019 – Proxy bias discussion.

qualitative.what_is_wrong: DI = 0.94 suggests mild disparity, but the privileged group has only 6 samples versus 194 for non-privileged, making metrics statistically unreliable.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Severe sample-size imbalance yields high variance estimates; a single decision flip could swing DI from compliant to critical. Small-group under-representation often hides systemic exclusion ([4]).
qualitative.how_to_fix: 1. Data augmentation: collect additional records for non-privileged foreign-worker status until n ≥ 30. 2. Use stratified resampling or synthetic minority over-sampling (SMOTE) before training. 3. Apply model-agnostic fairness constraints once data sufficiency is reached; otherwise deploy rule-based overrides to protect the group.
supporting_research: [4] Mehrabi et al. 2019 – Warns about unreliable fairness metrics on tiny groups.
[6] Kamiran & Calders 2011 – Shows benefits of re-balancing techniques.

result.cross_attribute_summary: All three audited attributes exhibit moderate disparate impact (0.82–0.94). While none cross the critical 0.72 legal danger zone, compound effects may stack: a young female foreign-worker faces the lowest approval likelihood due to intersecting moderations. Root causes trace to historical data bias and proxy variables. Recommended mitigations centre on (a) pre-processing re-weighing/DI-removal to neutralise correlations, (b) constraint-aware training (ExponentiatedGradient, PrejudiceRemover) and (c) targeted data collection to remedy extreme group imbalance. Continuous post-deployment monitoring should flag DI drift and intersectional harms.

reference_audit_spec.name: German Credit – Remediation-Ready Fairness Audit (cycle 2)
reference_audit_spec.why_this_spec: Credit-lending regulations (ECOA, GDPR-Art.22) care about both allocation disparities and error-rate disparities. The chosen metric set therefore combines: (1) legal disparate-impact trigger (DI), (2) selection-rate gap (DP-diff), (3) fairness in true-positive access and false-positive burden (EOD, AOD) and (4) overall utility inequity (Theil). Linking the quantitative picture to root causes and actionable mitigations makes the audit immediately usable by risk officers and model builders.
supporting_research: [4] Mehrabi et al. 2019 – Recommends multi-metric auditing and links each metric to a bias mechanism.
[5] Feldman et al. 2014 – Formalises DI thresholds and shows pre-processing fixes.
[6] Kamiran & Calders 2011 – Empirically validates re-weighing for credit data.
[3] Bartlett et al. 2019 – Shows real-world lending disparate impact, grounding legal urgency.

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Females receive favourable credit decisions at 86 % the rate of males (DI = 0.86; DP-diff = -0.115). AOD = -0.126 shows higher combined error burden on women.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Several German-Credit variables (‘personal_status’, ‘employment_since’, ‘other_debtors’) are historically gender-skewed proxies for income stability. They enter the model as if causal, but a causal path analysis shows they mediate structural wage gaps rather than individual repayment ability. Prior work finds similar appearance-based and gendered trust signals in lending decisions ([1],[3]).
qualitative.how_to_fix: Short-term: (a) run Kamiran-Calders Re-weighing on training data to down-weight gender-correlated rows, (b) deploy post-processing Calibrated Equalized Odds for rapid compliance. Medium-term: (c) refit using Fairlearn Exponentiated-Gradient with equal-opportunity ϵ ≤ 0.03 to close TPR gap, (d) introduce cash-flow variables (open-banking or transaction data) that are empirically gender-neutral, then drop ‘personal_status’. Long-term: (e) embed a causal constraint that blocks gender paths not mediated by on-time-payment behaviour.
supporting_research: [3] Bartlett et al. 2019 – Documents gender gaps in FinTech credit even after controlling for risk.
[6] Kamiran & Calders 2011 – Re-weighing reduces gender DI by 20-40 % in credit datasets.
[1] Duarte et al. 2012 – Trust cues linked to gender systematically bias lending outcomes.

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Applicants under 40 are approved at only 82 % the rate of older applicants (DI = 0.82). They also face a higher false-negative rate (EOD = -0.051) while older borrowers incur a 27 % higher FPR, suggesting mis-calibration across age.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: ‘Credit_history_length’, ‘savings_account_since’, and tenure variables act as strong age proxies. They capture lifecycle effects rather than intrinsic creditworthiness, producing indirect age discrimination forbidden under ECOA even if age itself were removed ([5]).
qualitative.how_to_fix: Data: (a) compute mutual-information between each feature and age to flag strong proxies; orthogonalise or bin-regularise those with MI > 0.15. Modelling: (b) train with Prejudice-Remover regulariser λ = 0.4 which Feldman et al. show can raise DI by >0.1 without major AUC loss. Policy: (c) set guardrail monitoring – trigger retraining when DI falls below 0.80 (high-severity threshold).
supporting_research: [5] Feldman et al. 2014 – Disparate-impact removal via orthogonalisation.
[4] Mehrabi et al. 2019 – Discusses proxy features and age bias.

qualitative.what_is_wrong: DI = 0.94 is within regulatory limits but computed on only six privileged-group samples, so one label flip could swing DI to 0.78 (high severity).
qualitative.why_is_wrong: The dataset under-samples non-foreign workers, likely because German Credit was historically focused on resident applicants. This size imbalance creates wide confidence intervals and risks masking true disparate impact ([4]).
qualitative.how_to_fix: Data: (a) collect ≥30 additional ‘0’-coded records or perform targeted data-sharing with another lender. (b) Until sufficient data exist, apply Bayesian hierarchical modelling with group-level shrinkage to prevent overfitting to tiny groups. Model: (c) during training, use stratified bootstrap or SMOTE-NC to balance, then validate fairness with jackknife CIs to capture variance. Deployment: (d) implement human-review fallback for decisions on the small group until statistical power improves.
supporting_research: [4] Mehrabi et al. 2019 – Highlights unreliability of fairness metrics under extreme imbalance.
[6] Kamiran & Calders 2011 – Shows synthetic sampling (SMOTE) effectiveness in small protected groups.

result.cross_attribute_summary: Every audited attribute shows moderate disparate impact (0.82–0.94). Though none breach the critical 0.72 threshold individually, their directional alignment means intersectional applicants (young, female, foreign-worker) face the compounded lowest approval odds. Root causes cluster around proxy features that leak protected-attribute information and historical under-representation. Remediation should begin with low-cost pre-processing (re-weighing, proxy removal) supplemented by fairness-constrained training, followed by strategic data collection for the severely imbalanced ‘foreign_worker’ group. Continuous DI monitoring with intersectional slices and confidence-interval reporting is mandatory to prevent drift into high or critical severity zones.
